title: As-of-right taxi licences in Victoria (2014)
design: Victoria against all other states, using only 2014-15, the one post-reform year before ride-share legalisation and driver GST registration. Method: stacked difference-in-differences, net of the same comparison for unaffected industries in the same states.
comparison: Treated: VIC. Comparison: ACT, NSW, NT, QLD, SA, TAS, WA.
grade_reason: Unlicensed UberX began in Melbourne in 2014, the same year, and only one post-reform year is usable.
headline: In 2014-15, the first year of as-of-right taxi licences, entry into Victorian taxi and road transport changed by −1.4 per 100 relative to other states (90% interval −3.4 to +0.9); exits by −1.4. Neither is distinguishable from zero. Unlicensed UberX arrived in Melbourne the same year.

category_summaries.competition: No detectable first-year effect. A rise in entry of more than about 0.9 per 100 in 2014-15 is ruled out.
category_summaries.prices: Descriptive only. Melbourne urban transport fares fell −10.7% relative to other capitals, most likely because of public transport fare changes from January 2015, not taxis.
category_summaries.productivity: Not measurable at division level. Shown for description only.

key_insights: The question: did as-of-right taxi licences in Victoria (2014) change how many taxi and road transport businesses started or closed?

The comparison: Victoria against all other states in 2014-15, the one year before ride-sharing and driver GST rules changed the market. Changes shared by every industry in the same states (a state's boom or slump) were removed by subtracting the same comparison for industries the reform did not touch.
What we found: no detectable change. Openings moved −1.4 per 100 businesses (90% interval −3.4 to +0.9) and closures −1.4 (−3.6 to +0.8).
How precise: a rise in openings of more than about 0.9 per 100 is ruled out.
What it means: graded Weak. Unlicensed UberX arrived in Melbourne in the same year, and only one year can be used.

method.estimand: The average change in the treated industries' entry (or exit) rate in the adopting states over the exposed years, relative to the comparison states, beyond the change for unaffected industries in the same states (VIC).
method.identification: Without the reform, the treated industries' rate in the adopting states would have moved as in the comparison states once state-wide changes shared with unaffected industries are removed (triple-difference parallel trends). Checked with the pre-reform event-study coefficients.
method.inference: No conventional standard errors (few treated states). p-value: two-sided rank of hat{β}^{net} among the P centred placebo estimates. 90% interval: hat{β}^{net} minus the 95th and 5th percentiles of the centred placebos (Conley and Taber 2011). Smallest detectable effect: 2.8 × their standard deviation.
steps: Took the treated industries (4623 Taxi and Other Road Transport) and the adopting states and dates from the register records; cohorts: VIC in 2014-15 against NSW, QLD, SA, WA, TAS, ACT, NT. Comparison states are those not yet treated in each cohort's window.
Built yearly entry and exit rates from ABS Counts of Australian Businesses (registered release vintage), 2007-08 on, pooling the treated classes in each state.
Drew placebo groups of the same number of classes from outside the treated division, matched on size (3931 businesses in the treated states in 2013-14); 43 qualified.

Design stage with every treated outcome hidden: checked the feasibility rules (at least 100 treated businesses and 19 placebo groups) and the power, then committed the plan (docs/pap_high_evaluability.md).
Estimated the stacked difference-in-differences for the treated group and every placebo group, and subtracted the placebo mean.
Checked each pre-reform year against its 95% placebo band, and ran the registered robustness variants (the other ABS vintage, employing businesses only, leaving each state out).
Applied the plan's decision and grading rules, with Benjamini–Hochberg q-values across the batch.
Prices: the same estimator on each city's CPI class relative to its all-groups index, against placebo CPI classes, with a registered variant that removes each city's pre-reform linear trend.
